common_name: Red Indian Guava (Historic Florida Pink-Fleshed Guava)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; Red Indian is one of the classic mid-20th-century Florida guava selections grown for its deep pink-red flesh and strong flavor.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after all frost risk has passed; Red Indian is an old Florida guava selection prized for its deep red-pink, strongly aromatic flesh and vigorous, heavy bearing habit. Fruit is medium-sized with a pronounced musky-sweet flavor that holds up especially well in juice, jelly, and paste making, in addition to fresh eating once fully soft. Like other guavas, fruit forms on new growth, so prune lightly after the main harvest to stimulate a flush of new fruiting wood for the next crop. Mulch heavily and expect some dieback in a hard freeze, but established plants typically resprout vigorously from the root crown.

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed; Copa is a South Florida mamey sapote selection grown for its very large, well-formed fruit.

directions: Copa is a Florida-grown mamey sapote cultivar valued for producing very large, uniformly rounded fruit with rough russet-brown skin and smooth, deep salmon-pink flesh of good sweetness and texture. Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with plenty of room for a large, long-lived canopy, and expect several years before first fruiting even from grafted stock. Harvest by watching for the characteristic color break beneath the scratched skin, then ripen fruit at room temperature for several days until it yields to gentle pressure. As with other mamey sapote, site it well away from structures, since mature trees become quite large and are difficult to manage once established.

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Key West is a long-cultivated South Florida mamey sapote selection valued for consistent annual bearing and smooth, richly sweet pink flesh of reliably good quality. Grow it as you would other mamey sapote: deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and room for a very large canopy at maturity, with several years to first fruiting from a grafted tree. Fruit should be harvested while still firm, using the scratch-test to check for color break beneath the rough skin, then ripened at room temperature for several days before eating. Established trees are tolerant of wind and brief cool spells but should still be given the warmest, most sheltered spot available outside true tropical zones.

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting in spring after all frost danger has passed, next to a sturdy post or trellis; in zone 9 grow in a large container that can be sheltered during cold snaps.

directions: Guyute is a widely grown collector-favorite dragon fruit cultivar known for producing exceptionally large, heavy white-fleshed fruit and strong, reliable yields compared with many other named selections. It sets fruit reasonably well on its own but produces larger, more consistent fruit when hand-pollinated with pollen from a different self-compatible cultivar, since flowers open only at night. Grow it like other dragon fruit cacti: gritty, fast-draining soil, deep but infrequent watering, and a sturdy post or trellis for the heavy, three-ribbed climbing stems to grip with their aerial roots. Protect the fleshy stems from any frost, since even brief freezes cause serious cold damage.

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting in spring after frost danger has fully passed next to a sturdy post or trellis; Vietnamese White is the standard commercial white-fleshed clone behind much of the global dragon fruit trade.

directions: Vietnamese White is the widely cultivated white-fleshed dragon fruit clone that anchors Vietnam's large commercial dragon fruit export industry and is commonly sold under this name in the US nursery trade. Fruit is medium to large with bright pink-red scaled skin and mild, sweet white flesh studded with small black seeds, and the plant is reliably self-fertile, setting fruit without a second cultivar nearby. As an epiphytic cactus it needs gritty, fast-draining soil, infrequent deep watering, and good air circulation to prevent stem rot, plus a sturdy post or trellis to support the heavy climbing stems as they mature. Hand-pollinating the night-blooming flowers still improves fruit size and set compared with leaving pollination to chance.

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; like other atemoya cultivars it generally needs hand pollination for reliable fruit set in US gardens.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Priestley is grown alongside Gefner and Bradley in South Florida to extend the atemoya harvest window toward the earlier part of the season, giving home growers a longer overall picking period across the three cultivars. It produces the same rich, custardy, sweet flesh with tropical vanilla and pineapple notes typical of the genus, and like other atemoyas benefits greatly from hand pollination with a small brush, since its natural beetle pollinators are absent in most US growing areas. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the segmented skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature for a day or two before eating.

common_name: Dasheri Mango (Classic North Indian Fiberless Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Dasheri is a classic North Indian mango cultivar grown worldwide in warm, frost-free collections.

directions: Dasheri is one of the oldest and most celebrated mango cultivars of North India, tracing to the Malihabad region near Lucknow, where a famous original mother tree grew for well over a century. Fruit is elongated and slightly curved with thin, greenish-yellow skin that stays pale even fully ripe, enclosing fiberless, intensely sweet, aromatic flesh with a small, flat seed. The tree is moderately vigorous with a somewhat spreading habit and bears mid-season, after many of the earlier Florida-bred cultivars have finished. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and complete frost protection, and reduce irrigation slightly as fruit nears harvest to concentrate sweetness.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Langra is a long-cultivated North Indian mango heirloom suited to warm, frost-free collector gardens.

directions: Langra is a historic mango cultivar from the Varanasi region of North India, named for the original grower, and is unusual among mangoes for keeping its green skin color even when the fruit is fully ripe and ready to eat. The fiberless flesh is sweet with a pleasant tang and a distinctive strong aroma, making it a favorite for fresh eating as well as pulp and juice. Trees are moderately vigorous and biennial-bearing in some climates, ripening mid-to-late in the mango season. Provide full sun, deep well-drained soil, and complete protection from any frost, since this is a true tropical cultivar with no cold tolerance to speak of.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops
